The black marlin (Istiompax indica) is among the largest pelagic teleosts, with adults attaining a lower jaw fork length (LJFL) of 401 centimeters [Li = 401 centimeters] according to records derived from converted fork length data. Females dominate the upper size range, and this ultimate length likely represents the maximum achievable under natural oceanic conditions. Complementing this extreme size, the ultimate wet weight of the species reaches approximately 750,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 750,000 grams], placing it among the heaviest of the billfishes. These massive dimensions are supported by a pelagic lifestyle that involves extensive migrations across tropical and subtropical waters, where individuals exploit rich foraging grounds to sustain such substantial somatic growth. Comparative studies within the Istiophoridae indicate that only the closely related Indo-Pacific blue marlin approaches this combination of length and mass, underscoring the black marlin's position as an apex predator in the epipelagic zone. The attainment of these extreme measurements is thought to require decades of continuous feeding and favorable environmental conditions, making large individuals relatively rare in fishery-independent surveys.

Sexual maturation in black marlin is characterized by the attainment of a relatively large body size, with puberty occurring at a lower jaw fork length of 217 centimeters [Lp = 217 centimeters]. This length, derived from eye-fork length conversions, marks the onset of gonadal development and the transition to reproductive competence. Individuals below this threshold typically exhibit immature gonads, while those exceeding it display active gametogenesis and are capable of participating in spawning aggregations. The size at puberty suggests a protracted juvenile phase during which the fish must accumulate sufficient somatic tissue to support the metabolic demands of reproduction. In comparison to other istiophorids, this length-at-maturity is intermediate, reflecting a life-history strategy that balances the benefits of early reproduction against the advantages of continued somatic growth. Field studies in the Coral Sea have confirmed that females caught at lengths well below this threshold rarely show signs of ovarian development, supporting the validity of this estimate for defining the reproductive population.

Reproductive output in black marlin is extraordinarily high, reflecting a broadcast spawning strategy typical of large pelagic teleosts. At a water temperature of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C], females produce approximately 260 million eggs per year [Ri = approximately 260 million eggs per year] across a protracted spawning season. This immense fecundity is thought to compensate for high rates of egg and larval mortality in the open ocean, where predation and advection into unsuitable habitats drastically reduce survival. The annual reproductive cycle, which may involve multiple spawning events, is supported by the large body size of mature females, which provides ample coelomic space for ovarian development. Available data suggest that this maximum reproductive rate is achieved only under optimal thermal conditions, as cooler waters have been linked to reduced spawning frequencies and lower fecundity per event. The thermal sensitivity of reproduction highlights the potential vulnerability of black marlin to ocean warming, which could alter the timing and success of spawning.

The initial life stage of black marlin is marked by an extremely small birth size, with newly hatched larvae weighing approximately 0.000011 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000011 grams]. This minuscule wet weight is a direct consequence of the modest egg diameter, which averages around 277 micrometers, and reflects the pelagic larval strategy common among scombrids and istiophorids. The yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves during the first few days post-hatching, after which the onset of exogenous feeding becomes critical for survival. The tiny neonate is highly vulnerable to planktonic predators and to starvation if prey concentrations are insufficient, making the early larval period a bottleneck for recruitment. In contrast to species that produce larger, more developed offspring, the black marlin's high fecundity and small larval size represent a classic r-selected strategy within an otherwise slow-growing, large-bodied fish. Comparative data from laboratory rearing trials suggest that survival during this phase is strongly temperature-dependent.

Maximum lifespan estimates for black marlin, derived from mark-recapture studies and length-frequency analysis, indicate that individuals can persist for approximately 4015 days [am = approximately 4015 days] under natural conditions at a water temperature of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C]. This longevity, equivalent to roughly 11 years, places the species among the longer-lived members of the billfish family, though it is considerably shorter than the lifespans reported for some large tunas. The estimate is based primarily on males, which appear to have a shorter lifespan than females; limited data suggest that females may survive beyond this benchmark. The prolonged juvenile period and delayed maturation contribute to this extended lifespan by allowing individuals to accumulate size and experience before investing in reproduction. Understanding the relationship between temperature and longevity is critical for predicting how climate-mediated shifts in sea surface temperature might affect population dynamics and turnover rates in this commercially and ecologically important species.
